rubric.headline: Seat-based SaaS is the most exposed model in any portfolio: agents do the work seats were sold for, while incumbents with workflow lock-in and proprietary data are best placed to sell the agent.

automation.why: Support, QA, implementation and sales development are 30–50% automatable inside the company

moat.why: Workflow lock-in and customer data hold; the UI layer does not

pricing.why: Per-seat gives way to per-outcome or consumption; every renewal reprices

entrants.why: AI-native vertical apps ship at a tenth of the build cost

diligence: Seat exposure: the share of ARR priced per user in roles AI replaces (support, SDR, back office)
Agent roadmap versus shipped: usage of AI features, uplift in net retention, pricing migration
Gross-margin drag from inference cost and who bears it in the contract
Data rights: whether the company may train or fine-tune on customer data

rubric.headline: Growth is the easy part; durability is the question — model-layer dependence, inference margins, and whether the workflow wrapper survives the next model release.

automation.why: The product is the automation; the company itself is lean

moat.why: Workflow and proprietary data compound; the model does not

pricing.why: Outcome and consumption pricing from day one, volatile by cohort

entrants.why: Every model release lowers the bar for the next entrant

diligence: Model dependence: switching cost and margin at each model vendor
Gross margin after inference, by cohort, and its trend
Retention when the underlying model improves — is the product the workflow or the model?
Revenue quality: pilots versus production contracts, consumption volatility

rubric.headline: AI compounds the data advantages already there in underwriting, fraud and servicing; the threat is to the labour-heavy players (collections, KYC operations, call centres), not to the rails.

automation.why: Servicing, collections, onboarding and fraud review are largely automatable

moat.why: Proprietary transaction and repayment data gets more valuable, not less

pricing.why: Take rates and spreads are set by the market, not the software

entrants.why: Licences, capital and distribution still gate entry

diligence: Model-risk and regulatory posture for AI underwriting (MAS, RBI, APRA)
Cost to serve: operations headcount per account and its trajectory
Fraud and credit-loss trends against the AI investment
Data exclusivity: proprietary transaction data versus bureau-sourced

rubric.headline: Revenue-cycle, coding and documentation are where AI lands first: a margin tailwind for owners who automate, an existential pricing problem for labour-arbitrage BPOs that do not.

automation.why: Coding, billing, transcription and prior authorisation are the first fully automated workflows

moat.why: Payer rules and clinical data access hold; the labour pool does not

pricing.why: FTE-priced contracts reprice to per-claim or per-outcome

entrants.why: Payers and EHR vendors can take the work in-house

diligence: Share of revenue from FTE-priced work (coding, billing, transcription)
Automation rate achieved versus promised; denial rates and days in AR as the proof
Payer and provider AI adoption that disintermediates the vendor
Clinical-data access and consent rights

rubric.headline: Proprietary data is the scarcest input to AI and the clearest moat — unless the product was the analysis layer, which language models now do for free.

automation.why: Collection, cleaning and reporting automate; curation still needs people

moat.why: Exclusive collection rights are the asset AI cannot replicate

pricing.why: Licensing to model builders is a new line; the interface commoditises

entrants.why: Scrapers and synthetic data test the edges of every licence

diligence: Where the value sits: collection rights and exclusivity versus the analytics UI
Licensing to model builders: a revenue line or cannibalisation
Scraping and fair-use exposure in each jurisdiction
Pricing power as the interface commoditises

rubric.headline: Agentic buying changes who the customer is: a marketplace that serves AI agents keeps its liquidity; one that relied on browsing and ad placement loses the margin.

automation.why: Listing, matching and support automate; supply acquisition does not

moat.why: Liquidity and transaction data still compound

pricing.why: Take rates hold where the marketplace clears the trade; ad yield does not

diligence: Take-rate exposure to agent intermediation
Share of discovery coming through assistants and LLM referrals
Data network effects that still compound
Dependence on advertising and listing revenue

rubric.headline: Traffic and attention are being re-routed through assistants: platforms with transactions and logged-in data hold up; those built on search-driven traffic do not.

moat.why: Logged-in transaction depth is the moat; reach is not

pricing.why: Advertising yield falls as the assistant takes the first click

entrants.why: The assistant itself is the new entrant

diligence: Share of traffic from search and its trend
Logged-in transaction depth and frequency
Content and user-generated rights, and AI licensing
Customer-acquisition cost under assistant intermediation

rubric.headline: The picks and shovels: AI demand underwrites capacity for a decade; the risks are power, concentration in a few hyperscaler tenants, and the price of capital.

automation.why: Operations are already lean; AI adds predictive maintenance

moat.why: Sites, power and permits are the moat, not data

pricing.why: Pricing power is up while power is scarce

diligence: Contracted versus speculative capacity; tenant concentration
Power availability and the economics of density (liquid cooling, PUE)
AI-specific build versus retrofit cost
Refinancing and exit multiples under rate scenarios

rubric.headline: Labour-intensive services gain margin from AI in the back office; the question is whether the gain stays with the owner or is competed away in price.

automation.why: Scheduling, billing, documentation and procurement automate

moat.why: Licences, sites and relationships; little data advantage

pricing.why: Gains are passed through where buyers are concentrated

diligence: Back-office cost base automatable within three years
Customer-facing AI that changes the service bundle
Workforce and regulatory constraints on automation
Pricing pass-through to concentrated buyers
